Father-of-two David Price, 42, was diagnosed with MS in 2018 after starting to struggle with his balance and peripheral vision. Eight years on, Price is preparing to attempt the record at the Manchester Half Marathon, but admits to feeling nervous. The current record is held by Chris White, who achieved a time of 1 hour 30 minutes and 46 seconds in Brighton in March this year. Image source, David Price Image caption, Multiple sclerosis is a disease that affects nerves in the brain and spinal cord 'Shock to the system' "It would mean the world to me to break the record," David said. "I'm not underestimating how much of a challenge it will be, but it would be absolutely fantastic." David, who works in IT, said his symptoms of MS first became noticeable in the office. "I was stumbling around the office and knocking things off desks. My peripheral vision and senses had gone a little bit strange and weird," he said, adding that he also "started to get tingling arms and legs." David described his diagnosis of MS as a "shock to the system", and something that took a long time to come to terms with. "Me and the wife didn't have a clue what multiple sclerosis was," David recalled. "It took me about three years to accept I had this long-term disability." title: Cash-smuggling gang jailed over £30m Manchester Airport operation

input.lead: The judge said the cash-smuggling gang 'revelled in spending obscene amounts of money'
input.summary: The judge said the cash-smuggling gang 'revelled in spending obscene amounts of money'
input.evidence_text: Cash-smuggling gang jailed over £30m Manchester Airport operation - BBC News Image source, National Crime Agency Image caption, The gang smuggled cash through in excess baggage, the NCA said By Mairead Smyth , North West and James Fell Published 2 October 2026 Members of a criminal gang who smuggled almost £30m in cash from the UK to Dubai through airports including Manchester and Birmingham have been jailed. Passing sentence at Bolton Crown Court, Judge Abigail Hudson described the offenders as a "shallow group of individuals" who "revelled in spending obscene amounts of money". The judge said those involved were "fully aware and wholly disinterested" that the cash they were transporting came from serious criminal activity, often drug dealing. The group used Emirates flights departing from Manchester, Birmingham and Brussels airports to transport criminal cash to the United Arab Emirates between 2017 and 2019. Sophie Logan, 31, formerly from Derby and living in Dubai at the time of the conspiracy, was jailed for seven years and six months. The court heard Logan worked closely with the alleged organiser, helping arrange accommodation, meals and nights out for couriers who smuggled the money. Judge Hudson described her trial evidence as "entirely dishonest and evasive". Heather Jeffrey, 58, from Bradford, was jailed for six years and six months, while Devanyl Graham, 27, from Dewsbury, received a six-year sentence. Lamara Noel, 34, from Bradford, was jailed for five years and Ben Royle, 32, formerly of Wilmslow and now living in London, was sentenced to four years and three months. Police later said Cravitz had died from multiple stab wounds, while Daulby was fatally struck by a stray police bullet fired at Al-Shamie. When I get there, the men are working in silence, hands sheathed in black gloves, bags of sweetcorn torn open, cardboard Just as I’m about to approach a vendor, I’m forwarded an email from a reader. It has the subject line The Mystery We All Want Solved "The reason I’m writing is because the people of Manchester are desperate to know what the hell is going on with all of the corn sellers on Market St "Why are there now so many of them? How on earth do they make a profit? Are they independent vendors or all part of the same company? Is their presence legal? What does their proliferation say about the state of the city centre?”

From a childhood in exile to surviving secret detention in China, his remarkable life and career have led him to global prominence. Using sculpture, installation, film, photography In Button Up! , the artist turns his lens on two centuries of Chinese and British relations. Taking inspiration from Manchester, a city at the heart of the Industrial Revolution, Button Up! explores how historic systems of trade, empire and exploitation resonate in today’s humani Conceived as a total environment, Ai Weiwei: Button Up! brings together new and existing large-scale works on display in the UK for the first time. The monumental installation features porcelain, cotton, glass, bronze and even buttons and toy bricks. Each material contains a stor Both global and personal, the title Button Up! is a playful poke at the artist’s ongoing battle with censorship. input.evidence_text: Finish work and unwind with live music from Manchester’s best jazz musicians. Beat the Jams live series showcases the very best of the jazz scene, at short rush hour gigs from 6pm at Band on the Wall. What better way to avoid those endless queues, chaotic traffic and stressful homeward journeys? Clock off and skip the rush-hour traffic while you watch live jazz and make the most of our happy hour deals from 5–7pm: £4.50 pints / 2 for £15 cocktails / £15 bottles of wine + pizzas from £5! The new season kicks off on 24 September with tenor saxophonist Dean Masser and pianist Richard Wetherall, followed by: 7 October – Anna Chandler-King Quartet Leeds based saxophonist and composer Anna joins us again for Beat the Jams, this time with her own band. Anna’s thoughtful and inventive compositions are firm favourites of us at Beat the Jams and her quartet promises to be a unique rush hour busting treat! 16 November – Sam Lightwing Quartet Saxophonist and composer Sam Lightwing brings presents brand new music for his thrilling young quartet, showcasing Sam’s original compositions, which blend classic mainstream jazz grooves with modern flavours of post-pop and latin, all wrapped up in the language of contemporary sax giants such as Chris Potter, Seamus Blake and Joshua Redman. 15 December – Svarc/Devine/Walsh with Richard Iles The band combines deep pocket, fearless interplay and a shared love of exploration. Expect everything from soulful melodies and infectious rhythms to moments of exhilarating collective improvisation, delivered with the chemistry that only world-class musicians can create. Tickets from £13 per show, or £42 for a season ticket

title: Is the funding market getting harder and what could that mean for Manchester? | Manchester Digital

input.lead: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing.
input.summary: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised
input.evidence_text: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised. More capital is being concentrated in fewer companies while the market for exits remains difficult Financial news recently added another dimension to that discussion. AI-related shares fell last week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower approach to the development of increasingly capable AI models. Nvidia finished the day down 3.4%, SoftBank fell 10.7% in Tokyo Additionally, the Bank of England is predicted to increase interest rates later this year, which could affect the North West's tech funding landscape by raising the cost of capital across the board, compressing valuations, pushing investors toward profitability over growth-at-all The British Business Bank's 2026 Small Business Equity Tracker found that equity investment into UK smaller businesses fell 4% to £12.3bn in 2025. Seed deal numbers fell 27% and venture deals fell 13%. AI companies attracted 44% of all investment into smaller businesses while the Beauhurst recorded £14.4bn of UK equity investment across 2,799 deals in the first half of 2026 but three AI companies accounted for 29% of all the capital raised. Those very large rounds can make the overall market look stronger than it feels to businesses raising at seed or Ser Beauhurst's analysis shows that UK equity investment more than doubled between 2017 and 2021 to £32.2bn while annual exits remained at around 400 to 500. An exit takes a median of four years from a funding round
